title: When the snow decides
bodyMd:
For a long time, botanists who studied mountain meadows assumed that alpine flowers followed the temperature of the air: a warm spring meant early flowers, a cold one late flowers. In the lowlands the rule works well. A team based at a research hut above the Susa valley wanted to find out whether it also holds at altitude, and concluded that it does not.

Between 2011 and 2019 the team fixed temperature loggers at forty points along a single ridge, twenty on the sunny southern slope and twenty on the shaded northern one. Every three days a member of the team walked the ridge and noted which species had opened its first flower at each point. In May the average air temperature on the two slopes differed by less than two degrees. Yet the gentians on the southern slope opened, on average, nineteen days before those on the northern slope, a gap far too large for two degrees to explain if the lowland rule were right.

What did differ between the slopes was the date on which the snow melted. Under the snow, plants sit in darkness at a temperature close to freezing, and they do not begin to grow until light reaches them. Once the snow is gone they grow quickly, and the team found that flowering followed the melt by a nearly constant interval, about three weeks in the case of gentians, whatever the weather in between. A warm spell over a thick snowpack advanced nothing; a cold snap after the melt delayed the flowers only slightly.

The finding may matter for the insects that depend on the flowers. According to earlier work that the team cites, bumblebee queens leave their winter shelters in response to air temperature, not to the state of the snow. In a year when a warm April wakes the queens while the northern slope is still buried, the queens might emerge to find fewer flowers than they need. The team is careful to add that it measured only the plants, not the bees, so this possible mismatch is a hypothesis awaiting a test and not a result.

The first paragraph says botanists long assumed that alpine flowers follow air temperature, as they do in the lowlands, and that a research team above the Susa valley tested this at altitude and found it does not hold. The second describes the study: from 2011 to 2019, temperature loggers at forty points on one ridge, twenty on the sunny southern slope and twenty on the shaded northern slope, visited every three days to note first flowers. In May the average air temperature of the two slopes differed by less than two degrees, yet the southern gentians opened on average nineteen days before the northern ones. The third paragraph says what did differ was the date the snow melted: plants do not grow until light reaches them, and flowering followed the melt by a nearly constant interval, about three weeks for gentians, whatever the weather in between; a warm spell over a thick snowpack advanced nothing and a cold snap after the melt delayed the flowers only slightly. The fourth paragraph suggests, citing earlier work, that bumblebee queens leave their shelters in response to air temperature rather than snow cover, so in a warm April with a buried northern slope they might find too few flowers; the team stresses that it measured only the plants, so this is a hypothesis and not a result.
